ai-at-work.title: OpenAI working on new $30B raise at $1.25T valuation ahead of IPO
ai-at-work.excerpt: Should OpenAI command an over $1 trillion valuation with this round, it would break records as the most highly valued private company ever.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: OpenAI is raising $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, which would make it the most valuable private company in history before going public. Digital workplace pros need to pay attention because this capital influx signals serious momentum behind AI tools that are already reshaping how we work, collaborate, and manage knowledge across organizations. Here's the thing though: valuation numbers that big tell us more about investor enthusiasm than actual product-market fit, and we've all seen that movie before.

ai-at-work.title: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’
ai-at-work.excerpt: Microsoft’s new AI diagnostic system beat generalist doctors on hard cases, according to a study in Science. But most of the improvement seems to come from the AI models underneath, not from Microsoft
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Microsoft claims its AI diagnostic system outperforms generalist doctors on difficult medical cases, though the actual performance boost appears to come from the underlying AI models rather than Microsoft's own innovation. Digital workplace leaders should care because this signals where healthcare IT is heading, and any organization managing clinical workflows or medical staff tools needs to understand both the real capabilities and the marketing narrative around AI diagnostics. Here's the thing: Suleyman's chasing "superintelligence" while the actual story is that he's wrapped a decent interface around existing models, which is useful but about as revolutionary as a really good dashboard built on someone else's database.

ai-at-work.title: Chinese hackers spied on thousands of companies after breaching IT giant ConnectWise
ai-at-work.excerpt: Microsoft points the blame for ConnectWise's breach at a China-aligned hacker, which relied on AI agents to rapidly hack into thousands of its customers.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Chinese state-aligned hackers broke into ConnectWise, an IT management platform used by thousands of companies worldwide, and used AI agents to rapidly pivot into customer networks at scale. This matters because your digital workplace runs on trust in third-party platforms, and when one gets compromised, the attackers essentially get handed a master key to every customer's front door. Here's the thing: we spent decades teaching people not to click suspicious links, and now the bad guys don't even need your help anymore.

ai-at-work.title: Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work
ai-at-work.excerpt: The ride-share giant previously deployed a much smaller pilot for ChatGPT Work but is now taking the enterprise agent company-wide.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Uber expanded its ChatGPT Work deployment from a small pilot to all 30,000 employees across the company. This matters because it signals how seriously enterprises are betting on AI assistants for everyday work tasks, and it gives digital workplace teams a real-world case study on scaling AI adoption at massive organizations. If Uber pulls this off without creating a support nightmare, other large companies will follow like lemmings, and if it goes sideways, we'll get another cautionary tale about rolling out shiny new tech before the culture is ready.

tools-tech.title: Remediation in the era of AI: Fix what matters first
tools-tech.excerpt: Every IT and security team knows the feeling of opening a vulnerability report and seeing a number that only goes up. Thousands of findings. Hundreds marked critical. A backlog that grows faster than
tools-tech.dwp_take: Computerworld reports that AI is flooding security teams with vulnerability findings faster than humans can remediate them, forcing a shift from "fix everything" to "fix what actually matters." This matters to digital workplace pros because an overwhelmed security team is a slow security team, which directly impacts user productivity when overzealous lockdowns and patches disrupt business as usual. Here's the uncomfortable truth: your security team has been printing tickets like a broken photocopier for years, and AI just cranked the toner to maximum.

tools-tech.title: The Patch Apocalypse is here. Patching everything isn’t the answer.
tools-tech.excerpt: For most IT teams, Patch Tuesday used to set the rhythm of the month. Updates arrived, teams tested them, change boards approved them, and deployments rolled out over the following weeks. It wasn’t pa
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft and other vendors are now releasing patches constantly instead of once monthly, forcing IT teams to abandon the old predictable Patch Tuesday rhythm. For digital workplace folks, this means your infrastructure stability depends on automation and continuous deployment strategies rather than scheduled maintenance windows. Here's the reality: organizations still trying to manually test and approve every patch are about to discover that security theater doesn't beat actual attackers, and five days is plenty of time for someone to ruin your week.

tools-tech.title: Rogue AI: When agents stop advising and start acting
tools-tech.excerpt: For the past few years, most enterprise AI has been advisory. It summarized tickets, drafted knowledge articles, and suggested next steps. A person still decided what to do. That’s changing. Agentic A
tools-tech.dwp_take: Agentic AI is moving from suggesting actions to autonomously executing them across enterprise systems, which means AI is now actually making changes instead of just recommending them. This matters because digital workplace teams need to understand governance, control, and accountability when AI starts operating unsupervised in your production environments. After three decades watching technology implementations, I'll say this: giving AI a credit card and hoping it doesn't go on a spending spree is how you end up explaining to the board why your entire workflow got reorganized at 2 AM.

tools-tech.title: Compromised security certificates blocked in Chrome, Firefox
tools-tech.excerpt: Private keys associated with eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by Indian digital trust provider eMudhra have been compromised, potentially allowing attackers to forge trusted certifi
tools-tech.dwp_take: Google and Mozilla have revoked trust in eight intermediate certificates from Indian certificate authority eMudhra after the company's private keys were compromised, meaning attackers could potentially forge legitimate-looking certificates to impersonate websites and services. This matters because certificate authorities are the foundation of web security, and when they fail, every organization relying on HTTPS and SSL/TLS encryption is theoretically at risk until patches roll out. Here's the thing: eMudhra probably isn't the household name that keeps your CISO up at night, but this is exactly why you can't just buy a certificate and forget about it, and why those browser updates your users keep ignoring are actually worth the five minutes of inconvenience.

digital-culture.title: Electronic Arts lays off 400 in latest blow to beleaguered gaming industry
digital-culture.excerpt: Electronic Arts (EA) is reducing its global workforce by 3%, or about 400 jobs, and shutting down BioWare, the 31-year-old studio behind the Mass Effect series. The cuts, announced yesterday, are the
digital-culture.dwp_take: Electronic Arts cut 400 jobs (3% of workforce) and shut down the storied BioWare studio following its September privatization by Saudi Arabia's PIF, Silver Lake, and Jared Kushner. For digital workplace folks, this is a reminder that even after a company goes private with fresh capital, headcount reduction and studio consolidation remain the default playbook when investor timelines demand quick returns. The irony here is thick: you buy a creative company for $55 billion to supposedly unlock its potential, then immediately start dismantling it because the math doesn't work fast enough.

digital-culture.title: Everyone’s taking PTO and sick days to play ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’
digital-culture.excerpt: Folks are lining up for their annual seasonal vaccines. But there’s one contagion that a CVS appointment can’t immunize against. “GTA flu” is sweeping the nation—and many workers anticipate “catching”
digital-culture.dwp_take: Workers are calling in sick or burning PTO to play Grand Theft Auto VI when it launches on November 19, with some booking time off months in advance. This matters to digital workplace folks because it's a real signal about engagement, morale, and how people actually spend their discretionary time when given the choice. Look, if your workplace culture is losing to a video game, the problem isn't the video game.

digital-culture.title: Inside the Exclusive Nathan Fielder Interview
digital-culture.excerpt: This week on “Uncanny Valley,” we go behind the scenes of our Nathan Fielder cover story, unpack tech billionaires’ generous promises, and discuss the suspicious letters sent to US election offices.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Nathan Fielder got the Wired cover treatment this week, and they're spilling behind-the-scenes details on their podcast along with takes on tech billionaire promises and election office threats. This matters because digital workplace folks are increasingly caught in the crossfire between tech industry hype and actual governance, especially when billionaires start making public commitments they may or may not keep. Honestly, if you're trying to build authentic workplace culture, watching how tech leaders perform for magazine covers is probably the best cautionary tale you'll ever get.

industry-news.title: OpenAI Ran Nearly 2,000 AI Agents on Brain Data: What They Found in 32 Minutes
industry-news.excerpt: OpenAI used nearly 2,000 AI agents to analyze mouse brain-cell data in 32 minutes, uncovering possible links to neurological diseases for further study. The post OpenAI Ran Nearly 2,000 AI Agents on B
industry-news.dwp_take: OpenAI deployed nearly 2,000 AI agents to analyze mouse brain-cell data and identified potential neurological disease connections in just 32 minutes, a task that would have taken human researchers vastly longer. This matters to digital workplace folks because it shows how AI agents working in parallel can solve complex research problems at scale, which has real implications for how teams might offload analysis work in the future. The funny part is we're still arguing about whether AI will take our jobs while it's out here basically doing the work of a small army of neuroscientists before lunch.
